transcript:
Doctor: What have you come in about today?
Patient: My throat has been sore. Swallowing is a bit uncomfortable, although I can still eat.
Doctor: How far back does that go?
Patient: Three days. It started on Monday evening.
Doctor: How much is it bothering you?
Patient: It's mild, really. It's just hanging around.
Doctor: Have you used anything for it?
Patient: I took acetaminophen last night. That's all.
Doctor: Are there any medicines you react badly to?
Patient: Penicillin gives me hives.
Doctor: Anything else you wanted to mention?
Patient: No, the sore throat is why I'm here.

Doctor: What's been bothering you lately?
Patient: My left knee aches when I walk downstairs.
Doctor: When did you first notice the ache?
Patient: About two weeks ago, after a long walk.
Doctor: If zero is no pain and ten is the worst, where would you put it?
Patient: Two sitting here, but five on the stairs.
Doctor: What have you been taking or putting on it?
Patient: Nothing. I haven't taken any tablets or used a cream.
Doctor: Any known drug allergies?
Patient: None that I know of.

Doctor: Tell me what's brought you in.
Patient: This dry cough. It keeps interrupting me when I talk.
Doctor: Has it been a matter of days or weeks?
Patient: Six days now.
Doctor: How rough has it been?
Patient: Moderate. I can work, but I'm coughing through meetings.
Doctor: What, if anything, are you using at the moment?
Patient: A dextromethorphan cough syrup at bedtime.
Doctor: Is there anything on your allergy list?
Patient: I don't have any medicine allergies.
Doctor: Is there another symptom you want to discuss today?
Patient: No. I just want to talk about the cough.

Doctor: What's going on with your ear?
Patient: The right one feels full, like it won't pop.
Doctor: Since when?
Patient: Yesterday morning.
Doctor: Is that painful, or mostly a pressure feeling?
Patient: Mostly pressure. If you need a number, the discomfort is three out of ten.
Doctor: Walk me through any medicines you're using.
Patient: I take loratadine every morning for my seasonal allergies. I haven't used anything else for the ear.
Doctor: Have any medicines caused an allergic reaction?
Patient: Sulfa antibiotics caused a rash when I was a teenager.
Doctor: Does the fullness come and go?
Patient: It's been there continuously since yesterday.

Doctor: What would you like to talk about?
Patient: A headache across my forehead.
Doctor: When did it begin?
Patient: Sometime over the weekend. I honestly can't remember which day.
Doctor: How strong is it right now?
Patient: Seven out of ten. It's hard to concentrate.
Doctor: Have you taken anything for it?
Patient: Acetaminophen this morning. I don't remember whether the tablets were the regular or extra strength ones.
Doctor: Do you have any medicine allergies?
Patient: No known allergies.
Doctor: How many hours did you sleep last night?
Patient: I'm not sure. I kept waking up and didn't look at the clock.

Doctor: What's troubling you today?
Patient: A burning feeling in my upper stomach. It started after breakfast this morning.
Doctor: How uncomfortable would you say it is?
Patient: Mild. I can go about my day, but I notice it.
Doctor: What medicines have you used today?
Patient: None today. I take no regular medicines either.
Doctor: Are you allergic to any medications?
Patient: I don't know. My old chart has an allergy flag, but I don't remember ever having a reaction or which medicine it means.
Doctor: Do you recall what time you finished breakfast?
Patient: Not exactly. I ate sometime before leaving for work.
Doctor: And the burning is still there?
Patient: Yes, the same mild burning.

Doctor: Can you describe the problem?
Patient: My right shoulder hurts when I reach up to a shelf.
Doctor: How long has that been happening?
Patient: Nine days. I remember because it started on my day off.
Doctor: How would you rate the pain?
Patient: It depends. Barely one out of ten when I'm still, but around six when I lift my arm. I can't give you one number for the whole day.
Doctor: Have you used a medicine for it?
Patient: Ibuprofen a couple of times. I don't know the tablet strength; the bottle is at home.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Was there a particular movement that started it?
Patient: I can't remember one.

Doctor: What symptoms are you having?
Patient: My nose is blocked on both sides. It's been two days.
Doctor: Is the congestion mild, moderate, or severe?
Patient: I don't know how to choose between those. I can sleep, but I keep breathing through my mouth.
Doctor: Have you tried any medicine or nasal spray?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Do any medications cause you an allergic reaction?
Patient: An antibiotic gave me a rash years ago, but I can't remember its name.
Doctor: Was it prescribed here?
Patient: I don't know; it was at a clinic where I used to live.
Doctor: Are you taking regular medication for anything else?
Patient: No regular medication.

Doctor: What brings you here?
Patient: I've had a cough for four days. My mother heard it over the phone and told me all about her asthma again.
Doctor: How bad is your cough?
Patient: Mild. It's mostly a few coughs in the evening.
Doctor: Are you using any medicine?
Patient: No. My mother uses an inhaler, but I don't use one and I haven't taken anything for this.
Doctor: Any medication allergies of your own?
Patient: None. My mother is allergic to penicillin, which is why she always asks me that question.
Doctor: Have you had trouble keeping up with your usual activities?
Patient: No, I've been doing everything as usual.

Doctor: Tell me about the wrist problem.
Patient: My left wrist has been sore for ten days. I type a lot for work.
Doctor: How much does it hurt?
Patient: About four out of ten when I'm typing.
Doctor: Have you been taking anything?
Patient: I used ibuprofen yesterday. A coworker said they take naproxen every day, but that was them, not me.
Doctor: Are you allergic to any medicines?
Patient: Amoxicillin gives me hives.
Doctor: Was there something else you wanted to ask?
Patient: I wondered in general whether people who play tennis get wrist pain. I don't play tennis myself.
Doctor: Did anything unusual happen to your wrist?
Patient: No injury that I can think of.

Doctor: What are we looking at today?
Patient: This itchy patch on my left forearm. It's been there a week.
Doctor: How troublesome is the itching?
Patient: Moderate. I catch myself scratching it while I read.
Doctor: Have you put anything on it or taken anything?
Patient: I haven't. There was a bottle of cetirizine on the kitchen counter, but it's my housemate's.
Doctor: Do you have any medicine allergies?
Patient: No known ones.
Doctor: Did you bring the note you mentioned when booking?
Patient: Yes. It just says 'severe rash, three months, steroid cream.' I found it in a shared notebook and don't know who wrote it. It isn't a description of my arm.
Doctor: What can you tell me about your own patch?
Patient: It's just this one patch, and I first noticed it last Friday.

Doctor: What would you like help describing today?
Patient: I've had a dull ache in my lower back since yesterday afternoon.
Doctor: How strong is the ache?
Patient: Mild, maybe two out of ten.
Doctor: What medication are you using?
Patient: None. I haven't taken anything for my back.
Doctor: Any known medicine allergies?
Patient: No known drug allergies.
Doctor: You mentioned an article on the booking form.
Patient: Yes, it described someone with severe back pain who took tramadol for years. I was asking about the article, not saying that's my situation.
Doctor: Is there anything else about your symptoms?
Patient: The ache is the main thing. My brother has kidney stones, but I've never had them.

Doctor: What's the concern today?
Patient: My eyes have been itchy for five days.
Doctor: How bad is the itch?
Patient: Mild. I notice it most when I'm outside.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking?
Patient: I take cetirizine every evening. I used to take loratadine, but I stopped that last year.
Doctor: Anything else, including drops?
Patient: No drops and no other medicines.
Doctor: Are you allergic to any medications?
Patient: Penicillin gave me hives. Pollen also bothers me, but that's the reason I take the cetirizine.
Doctor: Have you taken penicillin recently?
Patient: No, that reaction happened years ago.

Doctor: What has been happening?
Patient: I've had a headache since yesterday. It's moderate, across the back of my head.
Doctor: Are you taking medication for it?
Patient: Not for the headache. I do take levothyroxine every morning.
Doctor: Any other medicines today?
Patient: No. I haven't even taken a painkiller.
Doctor: Do you have any drug allergies?
Patient: I don't have any known drug allergies. Codeine once made me nauseated, but I wasn't told it was an allergy.
Doctor: Is that a medicine you still use?
Patient: No, I only took it after dental work years ago.
Doctor: Anything else on your regular medication list?
Patient: Just the levothyroxine.

Doctor: Tell me about the skin problem.
Patient: I have an itchy rash around my ankles. It appeared three days ago.
Doctor: How bad is it?
Patient: The itching is moderate.
Doctor: What have you used so far?
Patient: Hydrocortisone cream once last night. I haven't taken any tablets.
Doctor: Do you have any allergies to medication?
Patient: I'm not sure. I once developed a rash while taking amoxicillin, but I also had a new detergent then. Nobody worked out which it was.
Doctor: Are you taking amoxicillin now?
Patient: No. That was years ago.
Doctor: Anything else being used on this rash?
Patient: No, only the cream last night.

Doctor: What brought you in today?
Patient: I have a sore right ankle. It's been four days since I rolled it stepping off a curb.
Doctor: How painful is it now?
Patient: Four out of ten when I walk.
Doctor: Are you on any medicines?
Patient: No regular prescriptions. I took naproxen yesterday for the ankle, though.
Doctor: Any known medication allergies?
Patient: Yes, aspirin causes hives for me.
Doctor: Have you taken aspirin during these four days?
Patient: No. The only tablet I've used was the naproxen yesterday.
Doctor: Is there anything else on your medication list?
Patient: No.

Doctor: What symptoms are you having?
Patient: My right ear hurts.
Doctor: How long has it hurt?
Patient: Two weeks. Wait, I mean two days. I was thinking about when I booked a different appointment.
Doctor: And which ear is it?
Patient: Sorry, the left ear. I keep saying right, but it's this left one that hurts.
Doctor: How bad is the pain?
Patient: Mild, about two out of ten.
Doctor: Have you taken anything?
Patient: No medicine for it, and I don't take regular medicine.
Doctor: Any medication allergies?
Patient: None that I'm aware of.

Doctor: What's been bothering you?
Patient: My throat has been sore for five days.
Doctor: How severe is it?
Patient: I'd say severe.
Doctor: Can you tell me what you mean by severe?
Patient: Actually, moderate is a better word. I can eat and talk; I'm just frustrated that it hasn't gone away.
Doctor: Are you taking any medicine?
Patient: Nothing. Oh, I did take acetaminophen before work this morning. I forgot about that.
Doctor: Any known allergies to medication?
Patient: No known allergies.
Doctor: Any other medicine this week?
Patient: No, just that acetaminophen this morning.

Doctor: What is the problem today?
Patient: A cough that's been going on for eight days.
Doctor: How troublesome is it?
Patient: Mild during the day, but the nighttime coughing feels severe.
Doctor: What medicine are you using?
Patient: Dextromethorphan syrup at night.
Doctor: Are you allergic to any medicines?
Patient: Penicillin.
Doctor: What reaction did you have?
Patient: Hold on, that's my sister's allergy. I mixed up our forms. I don't have any known medicine allergies myself.
Doctor: Do you want to correct anything else from what you've told me?
Patient: No. The cough really has been eight days, and I am taking that syrup.

Doctor: What brought you here?
Patient: My left knee has been stiff and sore for three weeks.
Doctor: How much pain are you in?
Patient: Around five out of ten.
Doctor: What are you taking for it?
Patient: Ibuprofen every day.
Doctor: When was your last dose?
Patient: I haven't taken any ibuprofen this week.
Doctor: I'm hearing two different descriptions of your use. Can you clarify?
Patient: I know, but I can't sort it out without checking the packets at home. I may be mixing up this week and last week.
Doctor: Any drug allergies you know about?
Patient: Sulfa antibiotics gave me hives.

Doctor: What is troubling you?
Patient: I've had a cough for three days.
Doctor: How bad is the cough?
Patient: Mild. It's more of a nuisance than anything.
Doctor: Are you taking anything, and do you have any drug allergies?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Have you been sleeping normally?
Patient: Yes, pretty much.
Doctor: Does the cough happen at work as well as at home?
Patient: Both, although I notice it more when the room is quiet.
Doctor: Is there anything else you want to add?
Patient: Just that it began three days ago, not last week like I wrote on the form.

Doctor: What would you like to discuss?
Patient: A dull headache around my temples.
Doctor: Did it start yesterday, or has it been there for a week?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: What have you taken for it?
Patient: I took acetaminophen this morning.
Doctor: Would you call the pain mild or severe?
Patient: Somewhere in the middle, moderate.
Doctor: Any medication allergies?
Patient: No known drug allergies.
Doctor: Can you tell me more about when it began?
Patient: I can't pin it down right now. I've had a very busy week.

Doctor: What has brought you in today?
Patient: My left shoulder has been aching for four days.
Doctor: This is severe pain, then.
Patient: I need to check what time my ride is coming. Sorry, what was the question?
Doctor: Have you used anything for the shoulder?
Patient: No, nothing for it. I don't take regular medication either.
Doctor: And I can assume there are no medication allergies.
Patient: I don't remember what the old record says.
Doctor: How would you describe the ache in your own words?
Patient: It's there when I reach for things, but I haven't decided what number to give it.
Doctor: Has it really been four days?
Patient: Yes, four days.

Doctor: What's bothering you most?
Patient: A blocked nose and a sore throat. The nose started a week ago; the throat started yesterday.
Doctor: Is the nose problem worse, or is it the throat?
Patient: Yes, especially in the morning.
Doctor: What would you say about how severe they are?
Patient: The blocked nose is mild. The throat is moderate when I swallow.
Doctor: Are you using a nasal spray or taking tablets?
Patient: I'm taking loratadine, one tablet each morning. No spray.
Doctor: Do you have any drug allergies, or is there a medicine you're worried about trying?
Patient: I'm worried about trying new medicines in general. I don't have any known allergies.
Doctor: Is there anything else about the timing?
Patient: Just that the throat is new since yesterday. The blocked nose was already there.
